bib.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Chapter 17: Frontiers

question: Which topics beyond the book's MDP framework (GVFs, options, partial observability, reward design, open problems, safety) matter most for the future of reinforcement learning?
contributions: General value functions and auxiliary tasks (17.1)
Options as temporal abstraction with option models built from GVFs (17.2)
Observations, histories and state-update functions; POMDPs and PSRs (17.3)
Designing reward signals: sparse reward, shaping, inverse RL, automated reward search (17.4)
RL, safety and the future of AI (17.6)

results.claim: A general value function predicts the discounted sum of any cumulant signal under a policy and a state-dependent termination function, so it need not involve reward.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Auxiliary prediction tasks sharing a network body with the main value head can greatly accelerate learning on the main task (Jaderberg et al. 2017); auxiliary examples: pixel change, next reward, return distribution.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Learned predictions can be wired by design to fixed reflex actions (Pavlovian control), e.g. a vacuum robot heads to charger when predicted battery-out probability is non-zero.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: An option is a pair of policy and termination function; low-level actions are special options; planning over a restricted option set can converge faster to a possibly sub-optimal hierarchical policy.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Option models can be learned as GVFs (reward part: cumulant R_t, policy pi_omega, termination gamma*gamma_omega; transition part: one GVF per terminal state), but doing so with function approximation is beyond the state of the art.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: State is a compact, recursively updatable summary of history, S_{t+1}=u(S_t,A_t,O_{t+1}); it is Markov iff it predicts all one-step observations; one-step prediction errors compound in long-term predictions.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: POMDP belief states are not recommended as an approach to AI because assumptions and computation scale poorly; PSRs ground state in observable predictions instead.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Heuristic: a state good for some predictions is likely good for others, so pursue many predictions to direct state-feature construction; the agent, not the designer, should choose the predictions.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Designing the reward signal is critical; RL agents can discover unexpected, undesirable or dangerous ways to obtain reward; designers often tune rewards by trial and error.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Adding supplemental subgoal rewards can change the agent's behaviour away from the goal; better leave the reward alone and initialise the value function, v_hat(s,w)=w'x(s)+v0(s), which Wiewiora (2003) showed equivalent to potential-based shaping.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Skinner-style shaping (changing the reward, and possibly task dynamics, as learning proceeds so the agent is rewarded often) addresses sparse reward and works for animals and in computational RL.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Inverse RL cannot recover the expert reward exactly (many rewards make a policy optimal, a constant reward makes all optimal), needs known dynamics and features, and requires solving the problem repeatedly.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Reward search can be automated as bilevel optimisation (inner RL, outer high-level objective, analogous to evolution); experiments show intuition is not enough and the agent's goal should not always equal the designer's goal when the agent is constrained.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Six remaining issues: online deep learning without catastrophic interference, representation learning, scalable planning with learned models, automatic choice of tasks, curiosity/intrinsic reward, safe embedding in physical environments.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Current deep learning is not well suited to online learning; replay buffers work around catastrophic interference.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: RL inherits the plusses and minuses of optimisation: reward misspecification; the designer will not know how closely the agent fulfils the intent until learning is complete.
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Mitigations named: hard and soft constraints, robust and risk-sensitive policies, multiple objective functions; also safe behaviour during learning, borrowing control-engineering practice (modelling, validation, testing, adaptive-controller stability theory).
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

results.claim: Simulated experience gives safe, cheap, fast, plentiful data, but real-world embedding is needed where simulation fidelity is poor, especially where human behaviour matters (education, healthcare, transportation, public policy).
results.setup: Sutton & Barto ch. 17, conceptual discussion, no experiments

limits: Conceptual; no experiments, datasets or numeric results.

Authors concede much is 'beyond what is reliably known' and beyond the MDP framework; combining options with off-policy function approximation is unexplored; no guarantees when the Markov property holds only approximately.
Written 2018: pre-LLM; says nothing on RLHF, reward models, preference learning or test-time search. Applicability to those notes is by analogy (reward misspecification, shaping, auxiliary tasks).
practices: Do not rely on informal reward tweaking alone; treat the reward signal as a parameter to be searched against a high-level objective (Sec 17.4).
Prefer initialising the value function with a prior guess over adding subgoal rewards (Sec 17.4, eq 17.11).
Use shaping curricula: start from a non-sparse reward and move toward the real one (Sec 17.4).
Use imitation or inverse RL when no reward is known but an expert is available (Sec 17.4).
Add hard and soft constraints, robust/risk-sensitive policies and multiple objectives to limit optimisation risk (Sec 17.6).
Learn in simulation first; follow control-engineering risk management when embedding agents in the real world (Sec 17.6).

terms.definition: a value-function-like prediction of the discounted sum of an arbitrary cumulant signal under policy pi and termination function gamma
Whatever signal is added up in this way in a value-function-like prediction
extra prediction or control task in addition to the main task of maximizing reward
a pair <pi_omega, gamma_omega> of policy and state-dependent termination function; a generalized notion of action
H_t = A_0, O_1, ..., A_{t-1}, O_t, the data stream up to an observation
a state S_t=f(H_t) such that histories mapping to the same state give equal probabilities for every test
distribution over latent states given history in a POMDP
Markov state defined as a d-vector of probabilities of core tests
changing the reward signal (and possibly dynamics) as learning proceeds, from non-sparse toward the target problem
recovering the expert's reward signal from the expert's behaviour alone
internal reward such as learning progress, novelty or ability to affect the environment; a computational form of curiosity

figures.caption: A conceptual agent architecture including a model, a planner, and a state-update function.
figures.why: Shows where state-update u, policy/value, model and planner sit and what learns from what (PDF p.8 = book p.466)

code.snippet: v_{pi,gamma,C}(s) = E[ sum_{k=t}^{inf} (prod_{i=t+1}^{k} gamma(S_i)) C_{k+1} | S_t=s, A_{t:inf} ~ pi ]
